items.question: How do you assess generative approaches compared with latent prediction models for building goal-driven agents?
items.object: Generative approaches versus latent prediction models for goal-driven agents
items.answer: I do think generative approaches have value. If you're trying to learn a good generative model, there's clearly a lot of social and intrinsic and maybe economic value. But to use it to build goal-driven agents, if you try and do it in this generative space, the type of uncertainty you have to model now has grown significantly. Latent prediction models are just focusing on prediction. Those are the approaches that are going to be significantly more efficiently applied by a learning goal-driven agent.

But to use it to build goal-driven agents, if you try and do it in this generative space, the type of uncertainty you have to model now has grown significantly.
Latent prediction models are just focusing on prediction. Those are the approaches that are going to be significantly more efficiently applied by a learning goal-driven agent.

rubrics.text: The response states that building goal-driven agents in generative space requires modeling substantially more uncertainty than using latent prediction models.
The response predicts that latent prediction models will be substantially more efficient for learning goal-driven agents than generative approaches.

items.question: How do you understand the gap between humans and machines in how efficiently they learn?
items.object: The learning-efficiency gap between humans and machines
items.answer: Me and my collaborators were working on self-supervised learning more generally, and really noticing there's this big gap between humans and machines in terms of how efficiently we can learn, right? Humans' brain runs maybe on the energy equivalent of an electric razor, right? And we learn from very few examples. You know, I could show you a single example of something, you can acquire and understand those concepts. Machines, on the other hand, require thousands of hours of training, tons of examples, very compute-intensive, to understand and acquire a concept. So this was a problem that we've been thinking about, me and my collaborators, for a few years.

items.question: Why did you see JEPA as a promising direction beyond your earlier self-supervised approaches for images?
items.object: JEPA as a general framework for learning from perceptual data
items.answer:
We proposed several approaches in literature. Even our own techniques focused, for instance, on learning from images and that sort of thing. They were relatively effective, published in the typical machine learning conferences or computer vision conferences that you would expect. But what we noticed was that our approaches and methods were very specific, a lot of very specific inductive biases tailored, for instance, to learning from images. And, of course, we want to learn from much more than just images. We want to learn from perceptual data more generally, like video, audio, and so on.

This is where we felt like maybe there's something here, we need to step back. Yann LeCun, our chief AI scientist, had proposed his vision for AMI, and actually he'd been talking about a lot of these ideas for a few years, even before posting his document online. So really, we stepped back and said, okay, what if we just try more generally? The idea behind a JEPA is, you know, you have two signals from your environment, X and Y, and they're related somehow. The idea is you want to predict encodings of Y from encodings of X. Again, a very abstract and general framework.

items.question: How do you think about the choice between predicting encodings and predicting pixels when designing an AI model?
items.object: Predicting encodings versus predicting pixels
items.answer: I mean, what's common is predicting Y from X directly rather than encoding of Y from X. The idea was really, like, you want to predict encodings because predicting low-level pixels is a much harder problem, much more compute-intensive. And you have to ask yourself what the goal is. If your goal is to build a generative model that can produce visually appealing content, that makes sense.
quotes: I mean, what's common is predicting Y from X directly rather than encoding of Y from X. If your goal is to build a generative model that can produce visually appealing content, that makes sense.

The response judges pixel prediction appropriate when the goal is a generative model that produces visually appealing content.

items.question: How do you judge the efficiency of modeling every visual detail when your goal is understanding the world, reasoning, and planning?
items.object: Modeling visual detail for world understanding
items.answer: For understanding the world, making predictions about it, reasoning and planning, how much do I really need to spend capacity modeling every single blade of grass, every single part of this plain blue sky or cloud? So it's not efficient. That was kind of the idea.

items.question: How did you approach turning JEPA's abstract prediction framework into something that could learn from images?
items.object: Turning JEPA into an image learning approach
items.answer:
What JEPA prescribed was doing this prediction task in this encoded or embedding space. The idea is you have an encoder, something that encodes your signal X and Y, and you have a predictor, something that can predict encodings of Y from encodings of X. That's JEPA. But then, what does that actually look like? How do you implement it? That's where we started thinking and identifying some of the research questions to start out with and how to start building up this approach.

Our first work along that direction was the image JEPA. We were trying to get this to work with images. The first question you ask yourself is, what are Y and X here? If you're trying to learn from images, you could say Y and X are just masked versions of the same image. I see part of an image, and I find predicting encodings of the other part of the image. Okay, that's great. We have Y and X now. We're specifying them using masking.

items.question: Why do you see learning through passive observation as a promising approach to self-supervised learning from images and video?
items.object: Learning through passive observation
items.answer: The idea is now we can learn through passive observation of large quantities of data. Of course, we want to do this responsibly, but it really does unlock a vast quantity of data, similar to what humans are exposed to through passive observation, because humans acquire a lot of their understanding of the world even just throughout the first few months of development.
quotes: The idea is now you can learn through passive observation of large quantities of data.

items.question: What do you find interesting about cognitive scientists’ studies of how children acquire concepts before language?
items.object: Cognitive scientists’ studies of early concept acquisition in children
items.answer: I find these tests that cognitive scientists do with children really fun: trying to understand, have they acquired object permanence, this idea that if an object is occluded, it still exists? Have they acquired, for instance, this understanding of motion consistency or shape consistency? There's been a lot of studies in child development, and you do see these concepts emerge within the first maybe 10, 11 months of development. A lot of them do, and that's before any capacity for language.
quotes: There are these really fun tests that cognitive scientists do with children to try and understand, you know, have they acquired object permanence, this idea that if an object is occluded, it still exists? items.question: How do you view JEPA’s contribution to bridging the gap between how humans learn and machine intelligence?
items.object: JEPA as a framework for bridging human and machine learning
items.answer: If we want to get closer toward bridging this gap between human-level intelligence, or how humans learn, and machine intelligence, we're trying to step back and really take it from first principles. That's what JEPA proposes, and that's where this research starts to make some progress and propose specific instantiations of this framework. It's not that this is the only instantiation or this is the way to do it, but it's kind of first instantiations showing, remarkably, that it does work.

items.question: How do you think about what embeddings actually contain when you're using them to learn from a signal?
items.object: The information contained in embeddings
items.answer: We're saying encodings of some signal, embeddings, and these embeddings could really contain anything, right? In the extreme case, these embeddings have done no semantic abstraction whatsoever, and they just contain the full signal X and Y.
quotes: We're saying encodings of some signal, embeddings, and these embeddings could really contain anything, right? In the extreme case, these embeddings have done no semantic abstraction whatsoever, and they just contain the full signal X and Y.

items.question: How do you think about the challenge of getting JEPA to learn meaningful representations from randomly initialized networks?
items.object: Bootstrapping meaningful representations in JEPA
items.answer:
That's really where the research part came in: how do we bootstrap this network? We're not really giving it any information; we're just giving it images or video, showing it masked parts. The network, the encoders themselves, are randomly initialized. We're not starting from pre-trained networks. The predictor itself is also randomly initialized. At the start, it's all kind of random. So how does the network bootstrap itself to actually learn encodings that are semantic and meaningful, so the prediction task actually makes sense, but at the same time eliminate irrelevant or unpredictable information?

You need two forces here. One is, you'll notice the network by itself, the way JEPA is set up, is incentivized to make the prediction task as easy as possible. If you encode everything about X and Y, that's a very difficult prediction task. On the other hand, if you make it super easy, you just output a constant vector regardless of whatever you give it. That's a very easy prediction task. The network is already incentivized toward making things simpler. The challenge is, don't make it too simple. That's where we leverage existing techniques from the self-supervised learning literature, more general techniques people have proposed for preventing what's called representation collapse. Representation collapse comes up in a lot of different settings and scenarios in machine learning and has been previously studied in self-supervised learning. We set up this architecture and tried to figure out how we can integrate previous or existing approaches for representation collapse to prevent these kinds of trivial solutions.

items.question: Why do you think training the encoder and predictor jointly is important in V-JEPA?
items.object: Joint training of the encoder and predictor
items.answer:
One of our hypotheses about the project was the importance of training them jointly. When you train your encoder, you have to ask yourself, what objective am I trying to train my encoder with? What is it trying to capture? If you train them jointly, what it's trying to capture are features that are predictive. That's where you eliminate unpredictable or irrelevant information, because it's only going to try and encode whatever is predictable.

That depends on a lot of things. Inherently in the world there is some irreducible amount of uncertainty, so that is probably going to be eliminated. But also depending on how much capacity you have in your predictor: is this a big network, is it a small network, what is its architecture? That also controls to some extent what the network is able to predict, and so that's going to influence what you end up encoding. There's a lot of dynamic factors that come together. That's why we believed it was important to train them jointly, and why it's important to figure out a lot of these little design details: the predictor architecture, what are you trying to predict from what exactly.

items.question: Why do you favor masking large chunks of images or video when learning semantic representations?
items.object: Masking strategies for learning representations from images and video
items.answer: If you take an image or a video and just mask out little patches here and there, the same way people used to do in natural language processing, taking a sentence and masking out little spans, if you do that with perceptual data like images or video, you don't really need to do a lot of semantic abstraction. You can pretty much predict these little missing regions just by looking at the neighboring visible regions, and you get really terrible representations. So that was another thing to figure out: what are you actually trying to predict from what? It turns out we want to predict these big chunks from the video or the image that are masked, maybe for the entire temporal duration of the video, because now the only way the network can predict what's there is if it does some kind of semantic abstraction and discards some irrelevant information, whatever is not predictable. It forces the network to produce these kinds of semantic embeddings. There's a lot of really interesting dynamics at play.

items.question: How do you think masking should be designed to help models learn semantic representations from video?
items.object: Masking strategies for learning semantic representations from video
items.answer:
I think it's crucial for learning semantic representation. It's the degree, but also how spatially or temporally connected these regions are, because if it's sparsely dispersed throughout the video, again, it won't work.

I think what you actually want to do—and this, I would say, is still very much an open research question, but my opinion about what you want to do—is mask out semantic regions in the video, essentially. You want to take the real semantic content, so we're not talking about blue sky or just fields of grass; we're talking about the objects and their interactions, even temporally. You want to mask out things where interesting things happen and ask the network to predict that. That's what seems to lead to more semantic representations and levels of abstraction.

I think there's lots of interesting connections to humans. We visually attend to a lot of different things, and if you look at visual attention in children as they develop, it significantly changes from the first month to the first 10 months to the first two years: what we choose to visually attend to and the things we see. It's clear that's an important component of the learning mechanism in humans, and probably something we should be thinking about when trying to leverage JEPA or general mask modeling methods for learning from videos and images.

items.question: How would you want an object-aware masking approach for learning from videos or images to work?
items.object: Object-aware masking for large-scale unsupervised learning
items.answer: I'd want to take inspiration from implicitly understanding and masking out where the objects are in the video or the image, but doing it without having to run this big pre-trained object detector network. Ideally, it's something that you would do in a fully unsupervised way, so we don't want to be bottlenecked by the quality of the object detector either, which requires—current object detectors, the state-of-the-art ones, require lots of labeled examples. items.question: Why do you see Transformers as a good fit for the way you've designed V-JEPA?
items.object: Transformer architectures and masking in V-JEPA
items.answer:
JEPA prescribes a more general learning objective, but there's a lot of tools that have been developed by the machine learning literature across various communities that we can integrate. In fact, we do try to integrate them into V-JEPA to explore how far we can push this approach with modern tools.

The reason we choose to use Transformers for the encoder is because of the fact that we're doing masking. That's how we chose to design the signals Y and X. In theory, Y and X don't have to be masked parts of a video. They could just be the same video but corrupted. You could take that full video and add some noise to a part of it, or apply some transformation to that video, maybe some temporal shift or slow-mo, or some spatial cropping, geometric or photometric augmentations. There's lots of ways to design Y and X. The way we've instantiated it in V-JEPA is through masking, but I don't think that's the only way to do it.

Once you're doing masking, one great thing you can do is leverage Transformers to get efficient learning. We mask 90% of the video. That means the Transformer only needs to process 10% of the video. We flatten a video into a sequence of tokens. Transformers on their own don't have any implicit understanding of spatial distance in an image or temporal distance in a video. That comes from how you take the video and convert it to a set of tokens. Given a video, we take 16-by-16 pixels across two frames and call that a token. Then we feed those tokens to the Transformer as a sequence or a set of tokens. If you want to mask 90% of the video, just drop 90% of the tokens, and you get efficient learning. That was a technique explored in the literature with masked autoencoders and vision Transformers, except they were trying to do their reconstruction in pixel space. Again, it was really trying to integrate lots of these tools. We don't necessarily want to rebuild the wheel from scratch or build in a bubble. There's a lot of great tools we can leverage.

items.question: Why do you consider query-based feature pooling important for using frozen video encoders across tasks?
items.object: Query-based feature pooling for frozen video encoder evaluation
items.answer:
Previously, the video community had mostly focused on, after training a video model, fine-tuning it end to end, and suddenly it's very task-specialized. You have one model per task. There have been works exploring how to leverage the same backbone across many tasks, but I would say the dominant focus in the community has been on fine-tuning and producing task-specific video models. What we wanted to do was ask: how can we push frozen evaluation? Can we do unsupervised pre-training and get a video encoder that understands the world to some level, then freeze it? It's never seen any human supervision or labeled data. Then we freeze that encoder and train task-specific models on top. Rather than having one huge task-specialized video encoder for every single task, you have a shared video encoder and a bunch of very lightweight task-specific models, like a single-layer or two-layer network.

The question is how do you take the output of your video encoder and feed it to these task-specialized models? The structure of the video embedding might be hard to linearly combine to solve a task, so you need a smart way to take that output of your video encoder, represented concisely as a single vector, and feed it to a downstream model. That's what query-based feature pooling is. A Transformer outputs a token for every single input token, so we have one embedding vector for every single input token in the video. Now we want to take that big feature map and convert it to a single vector that we can feed to a single-layer neural network. Previously, you would just average that feature map to get a vector. But if the structure of your embedding space isn't such that semantic concepts are linearly separable, this pooling is going to potentially destroy a lot of structure and not work very well.

You're learning a single-layer network that learns to pool this output feature map into a single vector. items.question: How do you distinguish fine-grained temporal recognition from more coarse-grained action recognition when evaluating a video model?
items.object: Fine-grained temporal recognition in video evaluation
items.answer: We also looked at other tasks like fine-grained temporal recognition. Those tasks are pretending to put something into something but not actually putting it in, picking something up, moving something down, moving something from left to right or right to left, up and down, pretending to throw something but not actually throwing it. Those tasks require a fine-grained understanding of temporality. You can't predict those action classes just by looking at one or two frames. There are a lot of video classification tasks where you have visual cues and can understand or infer what's happening by looking at one or two frames. We looked at those two kinds of tasks that require fine-grained temporal recognition, but also more coarse-grained action recognition.

items.question: How do you interpret the apparent limits on the length of video V-JEPA can handle?
items.object: V-JEPA's temporal range during pre-training and inference
items.answer:
I think what we do during pre-training is sample three-second clips of a video. Every time we give a model a prediction task, it corresponds to roughly three, three and a half seconds of video. We mask out part of it and ask it to predict the other part. That's pre-training.

For inference, when we come to solve downstream tasks, we do go up to 30 seconds. We can give the model 30 seconds of video, and it can make a prediction. But we haven't explored longer-range temporal prediction yet during pre-training. It's not necessarily that there's some inherent limitation of going beyond 30 seconds or something like that.

items.question: Why do you think extending V-JEPA to longer video timescales calls for a hierarchical prediction setup?
items.object: Longer-range prediction and hierarchical JEPA
items.answer:
The pre-training task itself was only focused on shorter-range prediction. Most of the video tasks that we look at, the action recognition and fine-grained temporal recognition, go up to maybe 10 seconds long. That's what we've evaluated. Future work is definitely to try and push this, especially since the learning framework is already pretty general and should be capable of doing it.

But there are new considerations. The way JEPA is designed, it's going to eliminate whatever information is unpredictable. If you try taking the same approach and giving it 10 minutes of video, suppose you have an efficient architecture that can process 10 minutes of video efficiently, and gave the model 10 minutes of video and said, predict what's going to happen over the next 10 minutes, you might get some different learning dynamics. Maybe what's predictable in 10 minutes is not the same as what's predictable in three or four seconds. What's predictable in three or four seconds is fine-grained motion, because probably it's going to continue along its trajectory. What's more predictable in 10 minutes is something a bit more abstract or semantic. Probably you want a multitask or hierarchical setup where you're predicting at multiple levels of abstraction.

We still do want that three-second prediction range, and the question is how do you combine that with longer-range prediction without destroying what you're learning at this scale? Yann has talked about hierarchical JEPA in the past. It's not something we've explored in V-JEPA, but I think that's where this kind of architectural idea would come into play: you want to predict at multiple timescales, and what you encode at those different timescales is going to be different as well.

items.question: How do you view the value of generative approaches compared with predictive approaches in machine learning?
items.object: The value of generative approaches in machine learning
items.answer: I just think my personal opinion is the value is different, right? If you're trying to learn a good generative model, there's clearly a lot of social and intrinsic and maybe economic value, even scientific value, in doing that.
quotes: I just think my personal opinion is the value is different, right? If you're trying to learn a good generative model, there's clearly a lot of social and intrinsic and maybe economic value, even scientific value, in doing that.

items.question: Why do you favor latent prediction models for building goal-driven agents that use a world model to reason and plan?
items.object: Latent prediction models versus generative approaches for building goal-driven agents
items.answer:
I do think it has a place, so I'm definitely not saying we should not be doing that. But I think if you want to build a model that can understand the world and build up a world model, understand it and use that understanding of the world for not just content understanding and visual perception, and more generally perception, but to use it to build goal-driven agents—agents that identify a goal and then use their world model to reason and plan and identify decisions, make a specific sequence of decisions to arrive at their goal—there I think it makes sense to focus on prediction.

If you try and do it in this generative space, I think it's too complex. Not that it can't be done, either, but I just think it's very inefficient. You need a lot of capacity, a lot of compute, and the type of uncertainty you have to model now has grown significantly. If you want your encoder to capture something predictable and you're trying to use your model of the world to plan and reason, there's a lot of uncertainty now that you have to capture and leverage to come up with a plan to achieve your goals. The amount of uncertainty you have to capture just grows exponentially, in my opinion.

That's why I think latent prediction models, or just focusing on prediction, are the approaches that are going to be more efficient. Not the only approaches—I mean, generative could work—but I think those are the approaches that are going to be significantly more efficiently applied by a learning goal-driven agent.

items.question: How do you see hierarchical representations addressing the conflicting information requirements of different tasks?
items.object: Hierarchical representations at different levels of abstraction
items.answer:
Learning is all about semantic abstraction, right? You have some input. What do you keep and what do you discard? That's really the question when we're talking about learning. What do you keep, what do you discard, depends on what you want to do.

Maybe discarding a lot of information and just retaining shape is going to be really good for some tasks. Maybe if I only retain object shape in my representation, then I can solve specific tasks very efficiently with one or two examples. Boom, I got the concept. But maybe now I have a task that really relies on color. I want to distinguish one color car from another color car. Maybe it's quite important to distinguish color, depending on a task. If you don't have color in your representation, that's a problem. Even though it's very good for one task, it's not great for the other task. Tasks, depending on the task you want to solve, often have conflicting requirements for what you want to contain in your representation.

That's the big question: what is the ultimate representation, what is this representation that's perfect for all the tasks you care about? I think what I've been arriving at is maybe there really isn't just one good representation. Maybe that's where the hierarchical part comes in. You need several representations at different levels of abstraction. Depending on the task that you care about, you're going to use representations of different levels of abstraction.

items.question: What role do you envision for the V-JEPA predictor as a step toward a world model?
items.object: The V-JEPA predictor as a step toward a world model
items.answer:
One thing we also want to move toward is, it's very practical right now that we as humans can train task-specific models on top of these representations. Maybe we choose the ones that are more suited for our task and apply them. But ideally, this predictor, or the world model, like the predictor in V-JEPA, can be seen as a first step toward a world model. It's able to model uncertainty and predict missing regions in a video or an image.

I think ideally we don't just throw that away after training. Right now in V-JEPA we visually probe it to see what it's actually learned, and we were surprised to see that it's capturing spatial and temporal uncertainty. All of our evaluations were focusing on the representation of the encoder. How do you evaluate a predictor, a world model? It's still a growing research area that a lot of people are thinking about, but it's not as standardized as representation learning, for instance.

What I think you want to do in the future is have these representations not only applied or leveraged by human engineers designing task-specific models, but ideally you would feed those into a predictor that can do the reasoning and planning on its own. Given all these encodings or representations, depending on what the agent is trying to do, this predictor or world model is going to be able to configure the output of the perception module on its own to figure out the right level of representations and how to leverage and use them for this task. So it almost automates that a bit more.

items.question: Why do you think learning directly from perceptual signals is important for understanding the world?
items.object: Learning directly from perceptual signals
items.answer: I think it's important to learn from perceptual signals directly. It's important that you're trying to predict, you're trying to learn directly from video, from images, from audio, from whatever perceptual modalities or signals that you have, because I think that builds a very grounded understanding of the world.

items.question: Why do you think language can be cumbersome for expressing perceptual concepts?
items.object: Language as a way to describe perceptual concepts
items.answer: I could show you a few examples of a cup, and you might understand it just from a few examples. Now imagine trying to describe a cup. It's round, it has this kind of shape, usually there's something inside. But that description is a bit too vague. Suddenly it becomes really cumbersome to describe these intuitive concepts in language. And that's just the example of recognizing a cup. What about interactions that have a temporal component to them, or some kind of understanding of intuitive physics? I think it becomes really complicated to explain some of these perceptual concepts and signals in language.

items.question: How do you see language fitting into a perceptually grounded world model such as JEPA?
items.object: The relationship between language, symbolic reasoning, and perceptually grounded world models
items.answer:
I do think it's important to be learning in a perceptually grounded way, but there are also lots of tasks we care about where we want a language interface. Transformers in general, I think, have good capability for symbolic reasoning. Once you have a discrete set of concepts, how can you reason over those primitives that you've already defined? But a lot of the visual perceptual world is continuous. We have continuous pixel spaces, kind of open and continuous. I do see an intersection of these two components coming together, but I expect the reasoning part—or at least maybe there's various levels of reasoning to talk about—and the lower-level, visually grounded, perceptually grounded reasoning about what's happening in the interactions, I think that would be happening from a model that doesn't necessarily have to have language.

When we talk about JEPA, for instance, trying to predict in the future, the encoder is going to discard whatever information is not really predictable. One way to make things predictable is to give the predictor, the world model itself, some additional information. Imagine a robot interacting with the world and trying to predict what's going to happen. You have information maybe about proprioception, how joints were moving. That's information the predictor can use to try and predict what's going to happen. It's almost the actions that the robot was taking. You can also imagine actions being encoded in text or language. The predictor is modeling uncertainty about the future given text or information about what's going to happen. I don't think they're necessarily orthogonal. I do see these pieces coming together. But for building a world model and understanding of the world, a model capable of visually grounded reasoning and so on, you do need to be learning directly from perceptually grounded inputs.

items.question: How do you think about whether JEPA’s predictor should be called a vision Transformer?
items.object: The Transformer-based predictor in JEPA
items.answer: The predictor is Transformer-based. It's not necessarily a classical vision Transformer, because it operates in latent space. Vision Transformers, as they're prescribed, usually have as part of their prescription how you convert an image or a video into a sequence of tokens. That's called patching, and that's an important part of it. The predictor operates directly on embedding tokens, so I don't know that I would necessarily call it a vision Transformer. All these architectures are pretty similar, and it is Transformer-based.

items.question: How do you think V-JEPA should be developed into a goal-driven agent capable of reasoning and planning?
items.object: Developing V-JEPA into a goal-driven agent capable of reasoning and planning
items.answer:
I think the first step is just showing that you get the perception module and an initial version of a world model. How do you get there? That's ongoing research, but I think it comes down to focusing a bit more on the predictor or the world model.

We mentioned early on that the predictor and the encoder are trained jointly, and a really important part of this framework is the embedding space. How do we even know that we can get an interesting or semantic embedding space? This first proof of concept is that we can leverage this approach, instantiate it in a specific way, and get very semantic embedding spaces that are just bootstrapped.

What we found, and qualitatively probed toward the end of the paper, was that this predictor, the world model making predictions in embedding space, was capturing spatial and temporal uncertainty to some extent. As you also discussed earlier, it's predicting an embedding space. What is this embedding space? What is the network actually learning? Even though the focus was a bit more on the encoder, to get there, using this predictor and encoder for now, building goal-driven agents, doing reasoning and planning, more focus needs to be placed on the predictor.

That corresponds to some things we had mentioned earlier: longer-range prediction at multiple timescales. The predictor doesn't just capture three to 10 seconds of uncertainty or information; it can capture information at multiple levels of abstraction, at various timescales. Also, identifying how to condition it: what kind of information do you give the predictor to make predictions about the future, especially in a goal-driven agent? You can imagine conditioning the predictor on your goal, or somehow propagating information from your goal back to the predictor so that it can make intelligent predictions that lead you to your goal. In short, there's a lot of really interesting research questions and ways to go. We have a proof of concept, a learning framework now, a semantic embedding space. The question is how do you beef up this predictor, enhance prediction on multiple timescales, condition on additional information, and build goals into this learning framework?

items.question: How did your commitment to reproducibility and open science shape your approach to video datasets when moving from I-JEPA to V-JEPA?
items.object: Reproducibility and dataset selection in the transition from I-JEPA to V-JEPA
items.answer: One of the big challenges was going from image to video. Even putting algorithmic components aside, though there were algorithmic components to figure out, just look at the current state of image datasets versus video datasets. Part of reproducibility and wanting to do open science was that we wanted to be clear about which datasets we were using: datasets that are being used and explored and well understood by the academic community.

rubrics.text: The response connects choosing video datasets familiar to the academic community with supporting reproducibility in V-JEPA.

items.question: Where do you see the biggest gap between video datasets and image datasets that needs to be addressed for future progress?
items.object: The gap between video datasets and image datasets
items.answer:
There's a huge difference in both size and quality. The first thing was finding the right data to train on, good data to train on. And the fact that it's so much smaller as well—these datasets are so much smaller than current large-scale image datasets.

To make future progress, we really need to address this gap between video datasets and image datasets. In image datasets we have large-scale, curated, well-understood datasets—people have inspected and probed them to understand what kind of content is there. I think we need the equivalent for video datasets, with transparency about what content is there, but we need to improve the scale and quality of this data as well. That's where I see a big gap in going from image to video. Efficiency, of course, is a factor, but we're already a bit more efficient than some state-of-the-art image models. It's not a huge jump in compute compared to existing approaches people are already using for learning from images.

items.question: How do you explain V-JEPA's training efficiency when learning from video?
items.object: V-JEPA's training efficiency
items.answer: When you get to efficiency, luckily the masking provides a big boost there. As I mentioned, because we're leveraging Transformer architectures and masking, if you mask 90% of the video, you only have to process roughly 10% of it. That makes a big difference in terms of efficiency. V-JEPA can train much more efficiently than a lot of state-of-the-art image models because of the masking, but also because our video datasets are shorter and we're using much shorter training schedules. The fact that V-JEPA is predicting in an abstract or semantic representation space means we need much less training than, for instance, a pixel reconstruction or generative model. That also helps make video more accessible for training, because learning is much more efficient.

items.question: How do you see multimodality contributing to the next stage of JEPA world models?
items.object: Multimodality as a direction for advancing JEPA world models
items.answer: Multimodality, definitely. But I think it's not multimodality for the end goal of being multimodal, because there's a lot of work trying to produce joint embedding spaces of multimodal data. I think it's multimodal to the extent that it improves and builds up a more semantic and capable world model. Beefing up the predictor, conditioning it with other modalities such as proprioception, audio, depth maybe, if you have depth maps.

items.question: How do you think incorporating more signals into JEPA should help develop its world model?
items.object: Multimodal signals for a more capable JEPA world model
items.answer:
Ideally, I want those signals to be broadly available in an unsupervised fashion, so you don't kill that aspect. One of the reasons the method is so scalable right now is it's fully unsupervised; it can just be applied to streams of video or images. That's something you want to retain.

The multimodal part, I think, is going to help build up a more semantic and capable predictor, capable of much longer-range prediction as well. That's where I think that exploration should come in. It's not necessarily building just a better video encoder because it's learned from audio. It's trying to build a more capable and powerful world model that understands more signals.
